Senses.Explanation: Literally "single, sole" (單) and "transmit" (傳): "transmit singly," attested 692 times in 211 allowlisted texts. Zhongfeng says Bodhidharma's coming west is "called single transmission and direct pointing" and "at first had no twists and turns" (謂之單傳直指，初無委曲). In another address he gives a direct local definition: "the four holy and six ordinary [classes] are each originally complete; this is called single transmission," then asks, "what is transmitted?" (各各本來具足謂單傳，傳箇甚麼). Frequent compounds are "single transmission and direct pointing" (單傳直指), "single transmission of the mind-seal" (單傳心印), and "single transmission outside the teachings" (教外單傳).
Senses.Note: The records place the term in lineage slogans, questions, and verse. One lamp record pairs, "Bodhidharma came from the west, singly transmitting the mind-seal; the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi did not know one written character" (達磨西來，單傳心印，曹溪六祖，不識一字). A later lineage statement says the flower-holding smile was entrusted as "single transmission outside the teachings" (教外單傳). The four direct-question occurrences and twelve "termed single transmission" formulas belong to this shared lineage wording, not master-specific senses.

Occurrences.Kwic: 所以達磨西來謂之單傳直指。初無委曲。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng calls Bodhidharma's arrival single transmission and direct pointing, adding that it initially had no twists and turns.

Occurrences.Kwic: 四聖六凡各各本來具足謂單傳。傳箇甚麼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's explicit local definition and immediate question: each is originally complete—called single transmission; what is transmitted?

Occurrences.Kwic: 達磨西來，單傳心印。曹溪六祖，不識一字。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lamp-record saying pairs Bodhidharma's singly transmitting the mind-seal with the Sixth Patriarch not knowing one written character.

Occurrences.Kwic: 故末後拈花微笑嫡付教外單傳。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A lineage statement says the final flower-holding smile was directly entrusted as single transmission outside the teachings.

Occurrences.Kwic: 單傳直指意，覿體露堂堂。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A verse says: the meaning of single transmission and direct pointing; facing the body, exposed openly.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to raise or take up singly. Chan records use the verb with an expressed object: a single word 'no,' the first phrase, the upward move, the command, this matter, or a hair-blowing sharp sword. They also oppose 'raising alone and handling alone' to 'dragging through water and mud,' and place 'raise directly and singly' beside the transmission outside teachings and not establishing written words. The public-interview shape remains visible when a monk asks how the master treats people while 'today singly raising the command' and receives a blow. The Chan-specific bend is this productive teaching-seat verb: what is singled out may be a word, phrase, matter, sword, move, or command. Because those nouns are different objects of the same transitive act, they do not require separate senses.
Senses.Note: Wave-plan frequency: 401. Searches covered paired contrast, direct/single formula, word-'no' instruction, sword formula, phrase/move compounds, and public interview. Family check with raise (提起), raise singly (單單提起), the first phrase (第一句), the upward move (向上一著), no (無), and the command (正令) supports one productive verb rather than a fixed category.

Occurrences.Kwic: 垂示云。單提獨弄帶水拕泥敲唱俱行。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Yuanwu's pointer contrasts raising and handling alone with dragging through water and mud, followed by paired knocking and singing.

Occurrences.Kwic: 教外別傳，不立文字，單提直截，究本明宗
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A sermon places direct single raising beside transmission outside teachings and not establishing written words.

Occurrences.Kwic: 單單提一箇無字，如靠一座須彌山。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The expressed object is one word, 'no,' raised singly like leaning against Mount Sumeru.

Occurrences.Kwic: 單提一把吹毛利劒。逢佛殺佛逢祖殺祖。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng's address uses the verb with a hair-blowing sharp sword before the inherited kill-buddha/kill-patriarch line.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to have blood under the skin
AlternateTargets: a person who can feel pain
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "to have blood under the skin." The phrase occurs 136 times in 96 allowlisted texts. The corpus states its working contrast directly: one must have "sinews in the eyes and blood under the skin, knowing pain and itch; not knowing pain or itch, how is that different from earth and wood?" (眼裏有筋，皮下有血，知痛知痒；痛痒不知，何殊土木). It is consequently used as a qualification for a monk or person addressed in the hall: "you people must have blood under the skin" (汝諸人須是皮下有血始得), and "if he has blood under the skin, he will certainly have another livelihood" (他若皮下有血，必定別有生涯). A garden exchange also keeps the literal body image audible: seeing a cook cut melons, the master asks, "which one has blood under the skin?" (那個皮下有血). Zen bends the bodily phrase into a recurrent test for someone who registers a touch or blow, while the records themselves ground that use in pain and itching rather than an imported psychological category.
Senses.Note: The literal anatomy and the idiomatic qualification do not require separate senses here: the records explicitly connect blood under skin to knowing pain and itch, preserving the bodily predicate inside the transferred use. “A person who can feel pain” is therefore an alternate contextual rendering, not an interpretive second sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又須皮下有血，知痛知痒。痛痒不知，何殊土木。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The text itself connects blood under the skin with knowing pain and itch, contrasted with earth and wood.

Occurrences.Kwic: 是汝諸人須是皮下有血始得。畢竟如何？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An assembly is told that they must have blood under the skin; the speaker then asks, “ultimately, how?”

Occurrences.Kwic: 他若皮下有血，必定別有生涯，免得郎郎當當遞相鈍置。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A prose comment says that if the monk has blood under the skin, he will certainly have another livelihood.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問：刈得幾个祖師頭？座云：三十個。師云：那個皮下有血？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a garden encounter about cut melons figured as patriarchs' heads, the master asks which one has blood under the skin.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to make a ritual bow or prostration
Senses.Explanation: The graphs join rite or reverence (禮) to bowing or obeisance (拜): to bow or prostrate oneself. The word occurs 9,933 times across 403 allowlisted texts. In encounter dialogue it is a standard bodily response after an exchange, including at awakening: Xuefeng, at Yantou's words, has a great awakening and “thereupon bowed” (便禮拜). It also marks movement through the public event: a monk “bowed and withdrew” (禮拜而退), another “bowed and returned to the assembly” (禮拜歸眾), and one “bowed, rose” (禮拜起來), and took up a sandal. The performers include monks, masters, officials, commanders, and an emperor; the emperor bows and then asks another question. The same act can be challenged—Mazu asks Preacher Liang, “what are you bowing for?” (禮拜作麼)—or immediately met with a blow. Elsewhere a commander bows and takes the master as teacher. The Chan deviation is observable encounter choreography: this ordinary ritual bow is recorded as a public response that may precede a question, return to the assembly, recall, strike, or teacher-student bond. The texts do not make those different outcomes different meanings of the bow, and this entry assigns the gesture no unstated intent.
Senses.Note: One ritual action is performed by many actors and placed at different points in an encounter. Actor, rank, and narrative consequence do not create different referents. Compare “thereupon struck” (便打), “thereupon applied the staff” (便棒), the hands-folded greeting (問訊), the parting salute (珍重), and the head-to-the-ground bow (頂禮).

Occurrences.Kwic: 言下大悟，便禮拜，起來連聲云
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Collection from the Patriarchs' Hall (祖堂集), Yantou section (巖頭; the episode is told in Yantou's chapter): Xuefeng (雪峰), at Yantou's words, "at these words Feng had a great awakening" (峰於此言下大悟), "thereupon bowed" (便禮拜), and "rose and said in one breath" (起來連聲云), "this is the completing of the Way at Mount E" (便是鵝山成道也). The encounter-dialogue bow as the response to awakening. Narrated case → MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 豁然大悟禮拜。祖云。遮鈍根阿師禮拜作麼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (景德傳燈錄), the (亮座主) (Preacher Liang) case: he has a sudden awakening and bows (豁然大悟禮拜), and Mazu (祖) says "you dull-root lecturer, what are you bowing for?" (遮鈍根阿師禮拜作麼). The bow challenged, not accepted. The same (禮拜作麼) recurs across the lamp/case records — the (亮座主) case again in X69n1321 (lb 0004c05), C078n1720, J38nB406, and the (無業) case (這鈍漢禮拜作麼) in X68n1319 — multi-source. Two-speaker raised case → MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧便禮拜，師乃打之。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (祖堂集), (德山) section; after the master says "ask and you err; don't ask and you also miss" (問則有過，不問則又乖) the monk bows (僧便禮拜) and the master strikes him (師乃打之); the monk protests "I just bowed — why strike?" (某甲始禮，為什摩卻打). Directly links the bow to the blow (便打) and shows the bow met with a hit. Dialogue → MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師便禮拜。潭云：「見什摩道理？」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (祖堂集), (德山) section; the candle-blowing exchange with Longtan (龍潭) — Longtan blows out the light (lb 0406b08: 龍潭便息卻, "Longtan thereupon put it out"), the master himself bows (師便禮拜), and Longtan asks "what principle did you see?" (見什摩道理). Instance of (師便禮拜) (153×): the master, not only the disciple, performs the bow. The acting (師) is Deshan; dialogue/narrated → MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 其僧禮拜而退師云且來且來
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄); the departure form — the monk "bowed and withdrew" (禮拜而退), the master calls him back "come here, come here" (且來且來). The same exchange recurs in D48n8939 (且來且來) and, punctuated (且來)，(且來), in J23nB134 and J24nB138 — multi-source. Dialogue → MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 統軍便禮拜為師。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (祖堂集), (雲居) section; the discipleship bow — the army commissioner first refuses to bow and sits facing him (統軍使不禮拜而對坐), asks "when will the world find peace?" (世界什摩時得安), is answered "when the general's heart is satisfied" (待將軍心足), and "the commander thereupon bowed and took him as teacher" (統軍便禮拜為師). The bow that seals a teacher-student bond (also 州主便禮拜為師, "the prefect thereupon bowed and took him as teacher," in the Huangbo [黃蘗] chapter, lb 0609b09). Narrated → MasterName null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 皇帝便禮拜。皇帝又別問
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Collection from the Patriarchs' Hall, the emperor “thereupon bowed” (便禮拜) and then asked another question. This anchors ruler and ceremonial deployment without changing the bodily-action sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧禮拜歸眾。乃云：「喜鵲簷前噪
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The monk “bowed and returned to the assembly” (禮拜歸眾), after which the master continued, “the magpie chatters before the eaves” (喜鵲簷前噪). This anchors the bow within public-interview choreography.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禮拜起來，收他一隻履
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The participant “bowed, rose, and took up one of his sandals” (禮拜起來，收他一隻履). The passage makes the bow-and-rise bodily sequence explicit.
